CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER · OCTOBER

Percentages in everyday life and interest

“Everything 30% cheaper!”, “plus 19% VAT”, “2% interest on instant-access savings”: in everyday life, percentages change a price or a balance. In this chapter you calculate with an increased and a reduced base value, with discount and VAT, with interest for a year and for days – and you see how compound interest makes a balance grow.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate price increases and reductions with the multiplier, backwards too
  • apply discount, cash discount and VAT correctly
  • calculate interest for a year and interest for days: an interest year has 360 days
  • calculate compound interest year by year, with a spreadsheet too

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Price increase, price reduction, VAT

A jumper for €60 is reduced by 30%. You can work out the discount (€18) and subtract it (€42). It is quicker like this: after the reduction you still pay $100\% - 30\% = 70\%$ of the old price, so $60 \cdot 0.7 = 42$ €.

If a value is increased by $p\%$, you get the increased base value: $G \cdot (1 + \tfrac{p}{100})$. If it is reduced by $p\%$, you get the reduced base value: $G \cdot (1 - \tfrac{p}{100})$. The number in the brackets is called the multiplier.

VAT (value added tax) is added to the net price: in Germany usually 19%, for food and books 7%. The final price is called the gross price. Backwards, you divide by the multiplier.

KEY POINT · INCREASED AND REDUCED BASE VALUE

Increase by $p\%$: new value $= G \cdot \left(1 + \dfrac{p}{100}\right)$   ·   Reduction by $p\%$: new value $= G \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{p}{100}\right)$

VAT 19%: gross $=$ net $\cdot\, 1.19$   ·   net $=$ gross $: 1.19$

Backwards always divide by the multiplier – never subtract the percentage of the new value.

Discount is a price reduction, cash discount a reduction for paying quickly, often 2% or 3%.

By and to: “reduced by 20%” means the new price is 80% of the old one. “Reduced to 20%” means it is only a fifth.

INTERACTIVE · BY AND TO

Set an increase or a reduction. The strip shows the old and the new value, and the multiplier is below it.

EXAMPLE 1 · VAT

A bike costs €400 net. 19% VAT is added. What is the final price?

$400 \cdot 1.19 = 476$. The tax itself is €76.

€476

EXAMPLE 2 · BACKWARDS

After a 25% discount a jacket costs €48. What did it cost before?

€48 is 75% of the old price: $48 : 0.75 = 64$. Check: $64 \cdot 0.75 = 48$ ✓

€64 – not €60!

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Interest for a year and for days

If you put money into a savings account, you lend it to the bank. In return you get interest. If you borrow money, you pay interest. Calculating interest is calculating percentages with new names.

The capital $K$ is the base value, the interest rate $p\%$ applies for one year, and the interest $Z$ is the percentage amount. If the money is only there for a few days or months, you only get the matching part of the interest for the year.

Banks usually calculate with an interest year of 360 days and with 30 days per month. So three months are 90 days, a quarter of the year.

KEY POINT · INTEREST

Interest for a year: $Z = K \cdot \dfrac{p}{100}$

Interest for $t$ days: $Z = K \cdot \dfrac{p}{100} \cdot \dfrac{t}{360}$   ·   for $m$ months: $\cdot \dfrac{m}{12}$

Overdraft: if you overdraw your current account, you often pay more than 10% interest a year – much more than a savings account brings in.

Rounding: only round to whole cents at the end.

INTERACTIVE · INTEREST FOR A FEW DAYS

Set the capital, the interest rate and the days. The bars show the interest for the year and the part for the days you have chosen.

EXAMPLE 3 · THREE MONTHS

€2400 are invested for 90 days at 3%. How much interest is there?

Interest for the year $2400 \cdot 0.03 = 72$ €. For 90 days a quarter of that.

€18

EXAMPLE 4 · OVERDRAFT

An account is €500 overdrawn for 30 days. The bank charges 12% interest. What does that cost?

$500 \cdot 0.12 \cdot \dfrac{30}{360} = 60 \cdot \dfrac{1}{12} = 5$

€5

EXERCISES

Calculate the interest for a year: a) €1500 at 2%   b) €850 at 4%   c) €12,000 at 1.5%

a) €30   b) €34   c) €180

€800 are invested for 4 months at 2.5%. How much interest is there?

Interest for the year €20, for 4 months $20 \cdot \tfrac{4}{12} \approx 6.67$ €.

a) €3000 bring in €75 interest in a year. What is the interest rate?   b) At 1.5% there is €45 interest a year. How big is the capital?

a) $\tfrac{75}{3000} = 0.025 = 2.5\%$   b) $45 : 1.5 \cdot 100 = 3000$ €

€1200 at 3% bring in €9 interest. For how many days was the money in the account?

Interest for the year €36. $\tfrac{9}{36} = \tfrac14$ of the year, so 90 days.

Jonas buys a phone for €600 in instalments. He pays €104 for 6 months. How much more does he pay? Roughly what yearly interest rate does that correspond to if you calculate as if the whole €600 were borrowed for half a year?

$6 \cdot 104 = 624$ €, so €24 more. For half a year, €24 of €600 is exactly 4%, so for a whole year about 8%. (In fact it is more, because the debt gets smaller every month.)

TEST YOURSELF!

Interest for a year on €2400 at 3%?

$2400 \cdot 0.03 = 72$

€3600 at 2% for 90 days: interest in €?

$72 \cdot \tfrac14 = 18$

€3000 bring in €75 a year. Interest rate in %?

$\tfrac{75}{3000} = 0.025$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Compound interest and spreadsheets

If you leave the interest in the account, it earns interest too the next year. You get interest on interest: compound interest. The balance grows a little faster every year.

At 3%, the capital is multiplied by the multiplier 1.03 every year: €1000 becomes €1030, then $1030 \cdot 1.03 = 1060.90$ € and so on. Without compound interest only €30 would be added each year.

With a spreadsheet this is quick: cell B2 holds the starting capital, B3 the formula =B2*1.03. You drag this formula down.

KEY POINT · COMPOUND INTEREST

Year by year: new capital $=$ old capital $\cdot \left(1 + \dfrac{p}{100}\right)$

After $n$ years: $K_n = K_0 \cdot \left(1 + \dfrac{p}{100}\right)^n$

Rule of thumb: at $p\%$ interest, a balance doubles in about $72 : p$ years.

Spreadsheet: the point in “1.03” is right in English programs; on German computers the spreadsheet wants a comma.

INTERACTIVE · WITH AND WITHOUT COMPOUND INTEREST

Compare the growth with and without compound interest. After how many years has the capital doubled? You will learn the formula with “ln” later – here the rule of thumb is enough.

EXAMPLE 5 · THREE YEARS

€1000 is invested at 3%. How much is it after 3 years?

€1030 → €1060.90 → $1060.90 \cdot 1.03 \approx 1092.73$ €. Without compound interest it would be €1090.

€1092.73

EXAMPLE 6 · TABLE

What does the table for €500 at 2% look like?

AB
Year 0500.00
Year 1=B2*1.02 → 510.00
Year 2=B3*1.02 → 520.20
Year 3=B4*1.02 → 530.60

€530.60 after 3 years

EXERCISES

Calculate year by year: €2000 at 5% for 3 years.

€2100 → €2205 → €2315.25

Which formula goes into the spreadsheet if the capital is in B2 and there is 4% interest?

In B3: =B2*1.04, then drag it down.

Compare after 10 years: €1000 at 6% with and without compound interest. How big is the difference? (Calculate with the calculator: $1.06^{10} \approx 1.791$.)

With compound interest ≈ €1791, without €1600. Difference ≈ €191.

Check the rule of 72: after how many years does €1000 double at 6%? Calculate with the table or with $1.06^{12} \approx 2.012$.

The rule says $72 : 6 = 12$ years. In fact: $1000 \cdot 1.06^{12} \approx 2012$ € – it fits.

A loan of €1000 is not repaid and is charged 12% interest a year. Use the rule of 72 to estimate when the debt will be €4000.

Doubling in about $72 : 12 = 6$ years: after 6 years ≈ €2000, after 12 years ≈ €4000.

TEST YOURSELF!

€1000 at 3%, compound interest: capital after 2 years?

$1030 \cdot 1.03 = 1060.90$

By which multiplier do you multiply every year at 4%?

$1 + \tfrac{4}{100} = 1.04$

Rule of 72: doubling time at 6%?

$72 : 6 = 12$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A book costs €18 including 7% VAT. What is the net price?

$18 : 1.07 \approx 16.82$ €

Shop A: 25% discount on €80. Shop B: first 10% and then another 15% on €80. Where is it cheaper?

A: $80 \cdot 0.75 = 60$ €. B: $80 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.85 = 61.20$ €. A is cheaper – you must not simply add discounts.

A town has 50,000 inhabitants and grows by 2% every year. How many are there after 3 years? Make a table.

51,000 → 52,020 → 53,060 (rounded). Growth as with compound interest.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A rule of thumb from the year 1494

In 1494 in Venice, the Italian friar and mathematician Luca Pacioli wrote a thick arithmetic book for merchants, the “Summa de arithmetica”. It was one of the first printed books on mathematics and also contained double-entry bookkeeping, as banks still use it today.

It contains a rule without a reason: divide 72 by the interest rate, and you know in how many years a capital doubles with compound interest. At 6% it is 12 years, at 8% 9 years.

Try it yourself: Check the rule for 3%, 4% and 9% with a spreadsheet. For which interest rates does it fit well, and for which less well?

Source: Luca Pacioli, “Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalita”, Venice 1494.
